MR. HOWARD-COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege about which I gave Your Honour notice earlier this morning. My question of privilege relates to the manner in which the rights and privileges of Members of Parliament are being infringed, notwithstanding Standing Order 58(14), by the way in which some hon. members and some committees function under that Standing Order. As everyone knows, Standing Order 58(14) provides that the estimates shall be considered and reported by the various committees, with the deadline being yesterday. If by that date committees have not been able to report to the House on their consideration of the estimates, the estimates are to be deemed to have been reported regardless of whether or not committees have considered or voted on them. I realize there is a citation in Beauchesne which says that until the report of a committee and the evidence have been laid upon the table it is illegal to refer to activities and proceedings before standing committees, but I think Standing Order 58(14) has come into effect since that citation was written and colours the situation somewhat.
The Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections had referred to it the estimates of the Chief Electoral Officer and held some meetings on the Chief Electoral Officer's proposed expenditures. A few days ago, on Wednesday, because no steps were being taken by the committee to hold further meetings and as the estimates had not been voted upon, at my request to the chairman the steering committee met and called a meeting of the committee for Wednesday of this week. The committee waited half an hour for members to appear. During the course of that time only half a dozen members attended, two members of the Liberal party, two Conservatives and my colleague from Regina-Lake Centre and myself. As there was no quorum, the chairman agreed to call another meeting last evening. The committee assembled again in the committee room. Again we waited for a long period and again only two Liberal members, two Conservative members and my colleague from Regina-Lake Centre and myself appeared.
It seems to me there was, if nothing else, negligence on the part of certain members of that committee in not attending and providing a quorum so that the estimates of the Chief Electoral Officer could be considered and voted upon and the committee provided with an opportunity, if it so desired, to make some recommendation to the House with regard to these estimates of expenditure or on some other matter related to them. I feel that what was almost
collusion on the part of the Liberals and Conservatives not to attend that committee meeting has resulted in the privileges and rights of members being infringed. Accordingly, if Your Honour finds I have a question of privilege I would like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin):
That Standing Order 58(14) be amended by substituting for the date May 31 the date June 15 for the purpose of allowing the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections to continue to consider the estimates of the Chief Electoral Officer for the fiscal year 1973-74.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT BY SOLICITOR GENERAL OF NEW PAROLE AND TEMPORARY ABSENCE REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members are well aware of public criticism stemming from the fact that some inmates, while on parole or

temporary leave of absence, have committed offences. Additionally, there have been serious questions raised with respect to both inmate grievance procedures and staff morale within our penitentiaries.
I should therefore like to take this opportunity to outline to the House immediate measures which will help prevent abuses of our release programs, provide for a more adequate means of investigating inmate grievances, and describe steps which will improve working conditions and morale of employees working in penitentiaries.
In recent years, both parole and temporary absences have played an important role in the process of rehabilitating inmates. Parole is a procedure whereby an inmate of a penitentiary may be released before the expiration of his sentence so that he may serve the balance of his sentence in society, but under appropriate guidance and surveillance to help him lead a law-abiding life. It is a transitional step between close confinement in an institution and absolute freedom.
In recent years, day parole, requiring an inmate to return to prison periodically, or after a specified period of time, has been widely used. The National Parole Board has granted day paroles for the purpose of enabling inmates to pursue specified educational, cultural or job training activities which were not available within the institution and which, in the opinion of the Parole Board, would assist in the inmate's rehabilitation. When the Penitentiary Act was amended in 1961 parliament conferred upon the Commissioner of Penitentiaries and individual institution directors the authority to authorize temporary leaves of absence for inmates for three or 15 days. It was intended that such leaves of absence, either with or without escort, were to be granted for medical, humanitarian or rehabilitation reasons.
Since 1961, therefore, inmates could be released to the community both under the authority of the National Parole Board or the Canadian Penitentiary Service. Because the criteria for selection of inmates by these two agencies have not necessarily been the same, there has been some difficulty. The differences in criteria arise not only because of the different statutory authorities under which they operate but also because the considerations that apply in assessing an inmate for temporary absence differ from those applicable to parole. Inevitably this has led to confusion in the public mind. Moreover, there are certain legal complexities that bring into question the operation of a large portion of the temporary absence program. The most difficult problem concerns what are commonly called back-to-back temporary absences, a practice developed in recent years whereby inmates are released on successive leaves of absence over an extended period of time, generally for rehabilitative purposes. I have therefore made the following decisions:
1.	In the future the Canadian Penitentiary Service will cease the practice of providing back-to-back temporary absences for inmates in federal penal institutions. This involves a change in the Canadian Penitentiary Service directives and does not require an amendment to the legislation. The Penitentiary Service will continue to operate a temporary absence program under section 26 of the Penitentiary Act to provide three and 15 day absences for
June 1, 1973

medical, humanitarian and rehabilitation purposes, with or without an escort.
2.	For those inmates who are now on successful temporary back-to-back absences or where in the future extended absences are considered necessary or desirable by penitentiary authorities, provision will be made for a greater use of day parole under the Parole Act. This will enable inmates to continue their education, accept employment, and generally pursue their rehabilitation outside the institutions.
3.	Legislation will be introduced at the earliest opportunity to amend the Parole Act to permit the appointment of ten additional ad hoc members of the Parole Board. These ten members will be assigned in teams of two to the five regions of Canada and will deal primarily with day parole and panel hearings in the institutions. This step will enable the National Parole Board to deal with a considerable backlog of cases that require detailed consideration, and simultaneously satisfy the new volume of decisions on day parole that will come before the members.
4.	The appropriate regulations under the National Parole Act will be changed so that an inmate will be required to serve one-third of his sentence or seven years, whichever is the lesser, before he becomes eligible for parole. Previously inmates became eligible for parole after they had served one-third of their sentence of four years, whichever was the lesser. Concern has been expressed that the premature release of inmates on parole contributes to an unacceptably high rate of parole violations, and that those who violated their conditions of parole previously are permitted to become again eligible for parole at too early a date. This change in the parole eligibility period will affect primarily offenders serving long terms, that is, of more than 12 years.
5.	The National Parole Act regulation will be changed so that those who have forfeited their parole will have to serve one-half of any new term of imprisonment or seven years before being again considered for parole. This will prevent an offender who has forfeited his parole by committing an indictable offence from being reconsidered for parole before he has completed a large part of his total sentence. Under the present regulation an inmate who has forfeited his parole and has his parole revoked is eligible for parole consideration after serving one-third of his total term of imprisonment or four years, whichever period is completed first.
The two above-mentioned changes apply to inmates currently in our institutions. I am mindful of the fact that some inmates who had been making good progress toward their rehabilitation in the community might feel aggrieved by these changes. Any such case could be favourably considered by the National Parole Board where justified because of special circumstances resulting from these modifications.
6.	Steps have been taken to increase the number of classification, visiting and correspondence officers within the Canadian Penitentiary Service, as well as those members of the staff who are concerned with the social development of inmates. More visiting and correspondence
Penitentiaries, Parole and Temporary Absence
officers will provide additional opportunity for family and friends to meet and communicate with inmates within institutions. Additional classification officers will ensure that individual inmates receive appropriate diagnostic and counselling service as well as providing for closer screening of applications for temporary absence, day parole and full parole. Social development and activity officers are required to enrich institutional programs of leisure-time activities. The steps that have been taken to improve programs within the penitentiary system have included, as I mentioned, the use of temporary absences and day parole to gain access to rehabilitative resources in the community for individual inmates.
7.	Steps are being taken to provide additional staff facilities, such as conference rooms, libraries, lockers, lounge and shower facilities, to improve working conditions for employees in our penitentiaries.
Programs of inmate rehabilitation cannot be achieved without good relations between staff and inmates. A great deal of effort has been and will continue to be expended on establishing the best possible conditions for the reform of the inmate, but I fully realize that where staff, for one reason or another, are dissatisfied in terms of their working conditions, the prospects of useful staff-inmate relationships tend to diminish. While it is true that the penitentiary service is now unionized and a collective agreement exists, there are other areas not subject to negotiation where we could improve staff conditions.
8.	To assure the impartial investigation of inmate complaints and grievances, I have received authority, under part II, section 6, of the Inquiries Act, to create the position of correctional investigator. Both the Archambault and the Swackhamer commissions recommend visiting committees to assist in the impartial consideration of inmate grievances. While I feel that this is a valuable suggestion, I am certain the creation of the correctional investigator's position will better accomplish these goals.
The appointee will assure that inmate grievances are dealt with at an early stage and on a basis that is satisfactory, generally speaking, to the inmate, the penitentiary staff, and to the Canadian public. The appointee will report directly to the Solicitor General. The correctional investigator's duties will be to investigate complaints of federal penitentiary inmates and to make recommendations concerning those complaints. The investigator will also be authorized to inquire on her own initiative but will be relieved of the necessity of making an investigation if she is satisfied that the complainant has not sought legal or administrative remedy. This official will be required to make an annual report to the Solicitor General who will table it in the House of Commons, subject to the deletion of any material that might adversely affect the security of Canada or any penitentiary, and the civil liberties or privacy of individuals.
9.	Miss Inger Hansen has been appointed Canada's first correctional investigator. Miss Hansen has broad experience in both the field of criminal law and corrections generally and I believe that her distinguished background will assure her success as correctional investigator.
These are recommendations that are calculated to deal with some federal correctional problems on a short-term basis in the field of penitentiary services, temporary

June 1, 1973
Penitentiaries, Parole and Temporary Absence
absences and parole. For the long term, more profound changes may be necessary. I should remind the House that there is a report of the task force on the release of inmates under the chairmanship of Mr. Justice Hugessen to be made public shortly which requires detailed consideration because it raises a number of important issues that could only be dealt with by substantial changes in current legislation. Similarly, a committee of the other place is conducting inquiries into the entire question of the release of inmates, whether on parole or temporary absence. Finally, there is the Justice and Legal Affairs Committee of this House which just a few days ago has assumed the task of carrying out an inquiry into our penitentiary system, including parole and temporary absence. All of these reports will be considered in depth as part of an ever-expanding development of federal corrections in Canada.
As I stated above, I do not contend that the policies I have announced today are the long-term answers to our problems in the field of corrections. In due course, we will have to deal with some of the other more complex questions, but these measures I have discussed are designed to provide immediate solutions for some immediate problems. They will, I hope, help to assure the public and parliament that this government is determined to demand both security and rehabilitation from our release programs, while at the same time protecting the rights of inmates and creating better working conditions for our penitentiary employees.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT BY SOLICITOR GENERAL OF NEW PAROLE AND TEMPORARY ABSENCE REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have just heard another example of government by ad hocery. The minister has reacted to public outcry as have others of his colleagues, particularly the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp). They have reacted with band-aid measures when they should be formulating cohesive and in-depth policies.
The minister cannot extract the penal system and the penitentiary system from the over-all problem of dealing with crime in this country, and that is exactly what he is attempting to do. He has made certain changes with respect to back-to-back leave and temporary absences. Does this mean that convicted wife murderers are no longer going to be able to obtain leave in order to marry their mistresses for whom murder was committed in the first place? Does this mean that criminals are not going to be permitted to visit such eminent institutions as la salon de la femme and then disappear? Does this mean that judges are no longer going to say at the conclusion of a criminal trial, I find you guilty and sentence you to two years, three years, five years, or whatever the case may be, but, instead, will be saying, I find you guilty and I have arranged for a reservation for you at the rehabilitation centre at such and such a place. Taking measures such as those that have been announced by the minister, instead of approaching the matter in a scientific fashion, in an in-depth fashion and considering the over-all fabric of crime and penal reform in the country, is no solution.
In my view, Sir, what the minister should have been announcing is a program aimed, first, at primary prevention; second, at early detection; third, at the problems of detention; fourth, at active treatment; fifth, at rehabilita-

tion and follow-up and, last, at education and research. That is the whole scientific package that has to be considered. The penal system cannot be viewed in a vacuum and extracted and band-aid solutions applied in the expectation that they will solve all the problems that exist. Government policies such as I have suggested in order to deal with crime in accordance with the directives I have listed would be an immense step forward. Our knowledge of man and his behaviour could be utilized within such a unified policy to provide a scientific basis for developing that kind of policy. Surely the knowledge we have in the various disciplines impinging on criminal behaviour and the measures deemed appropriate to control it could thereby be co-ordinated.
In his announcement the minister also failed to outline to us, and thereby failed to allay public apprehension in this area, the criteria for temporary leaves of absence that are going to be granted without escort. What criteria are envisaged in the granting and greater use of day parole? The elimination of back to back leave implies that a greater use of day parole is very likely to cancel out the former. What assurance have the people of Canada that the enlargement of the day parole process is not going to be so great as to eliminate entirely whatever improvement may be derived from the cancellation of the policy of back to back leaves?
With respect to the announcement concerning the National Parole Board, we wonder whether the enlargement of the Parole Board will permit the reinstatement of the interview system. When will this legislation be introduced? The minister has said nothing about that, given the government's new set of priorities as leaked by a secret cabinet document the other day, which does not include penal reform, I might point out.
The minister referred to serving longer sentences prior to becoming eligible for parole. Is any consideration given to the type of crime in the granting of parole? He said nothing about that. For instance, what will the procedure be regarding sexual offenders, murderers, habitual criminals and so on? Is any account taken of the response of the prisoner to rehabilitation efforts? How much consultation exists or is planned with the judiciary? There is precious little today. It is the judge who must decide the length of the sentence, not the parole board. Liaison is necessary, for example, in cases where the judge does not recommend mercy.
It is one thing to view the almost complete erosion of the morale of the staff of the penal system and another to try to correct it by the measures announced by the minister. The increases in staff mentioned by the minister will not solve the problem. They sound good, but the proof of the pudding is in the eating. Is the Department of the Solicitor General having success in recruiting persons for these positions? What ratio of classification officers tc inmates has been established as acceptable? These are the kinds of questions that arise in our minds.
The minister made an announcement with regard to additional staff facilities. We welcome this kind of announcement. Perhaps the staff will at least have the kind of luxurious facilities now available to inmates. Will
June 1, 1973

staff members be consulted on any new reform undertaken in the penal institution? Are there any plans for increased training facilities for penitentiary staff, an area which is crying out for reform?
With regard to the correctional investigator, I find no quarrel with the minister in so far as the appointment is concerned, if for no other reason than her racial background and the spelling of her name. Coming from the country which she does and settling in Canada, obviously she has to be of unusually high calibre as an individual. However, the announcement is woefully inadequate with regard to the terms of reference of this individual.
The status of the correctional investigator is not clear. She continues to be a public servant. Although the Solicitor General stated that the investigator is independent of any association with the Canadian Penitentiary Service, the investigator appears to remain a legal officer of the Department of Justice which is responsible for providing legal advisers to all government departments. The functions of these officers are under the Deputy Attorney General of Canada, another public official. Their duties are to furnish legal advice and obtain for officials opinions of the Deputy Attorney General for the government departments and agencies to which they are assigned.
It appears, therefore, that the correctional investigator, as a Department of Justice legal officer, always was and continues to be independent of the penitentiary service of the Solicitor General. Accordingly, the statement that she has been granted full independence is, in my view, rather meaningless. She has been and continues to be responsible to and under the direction of the Deputy Attorney General of Canada. She is not an investigator who is independent of the government and responsible to parliament and the public. Further, as a departmental official, all the reports of the investigator will be interdepartmental communications and subject to the rules of government secrecy as announced by the government in the House this session. subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT BY SOLICITOR GENERAL OF NEW PAROLE AND TEMPORARY ABSENCE REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want first to express my thanks to the minister for having made available a copy of his statement some time before the House met, even though its social implications and effects on the penitentiary service are more than could be grasped in the time available to look at it. My reaction is that it is a statement responding to a situation out of desperation rather than a clear approach to a fair and just penal system in the nation. It is a political document, not one with any penological sense to it.
I wish to deal briefly with the points raised by the minister. The minister referred to the day parole system and the so-called back-to-back or successive 15 day temporary absences that can be granted by the Commissioner of Penitentiaries. The minister seeks to dispose of that and not have any more successive temporary absences. He thinks that abuses of the system will accordingly be lessened or curtailed. The minister is under a misapprehension or misunderstanding. The problem does not arise because an inmate has a three day, 15-day or a number of 15-day successive temporary absences. The problem arises in the assessment of the individual in the first place.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT BY SOLICITOR GENERAL OF NEW PAROLE AND TEMPORARY ABSENCE REGULATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT BY SOLICITOR GENERAL OF NEW PAROLE AND TEMPORARY ABSENCE REGULATIONS
speechtext:
If the person who makes the assessment or selection of inmates eligible for temporary absence is incompetent or conned into it, there will be a continuation of abuses. Let me say that when it comes to conning, inmates have far more brains than most of the people in the penitentiary system.
The minister talked about expanding the Parole Board. I gather the purpose is that the additional members will permit the board to deal with the question of day parole and the great backlog of cases. One would think from this that the minister is curtailing day parole, but he is in fact seeking to expand and intensify it. This is fine, but the difficulty again arises with regard to the competency or otherwise of the person making the selection. There is also the problem of supervision in the after-care field and working with the inmate whether he is on temporary absence, day parole or full parole. In the absence of a concomitant community activity involving that individual, the prospects of failure will increase.
Again-and this points up the political impact of the document-the minister talks about establishing a seven year period instead of a four year period before a person will be eligible for parole. The minister seems, on the one hand, to wish to intensify the activities of the Parole Board and, on the other hand, to restrict and curtail those activities and to make sure that individuals stay in jail for a longer period of time. This is contrary to the idea of parole, contrary to the idea that an inmate should have an opportunity to live in a free society, in a free community to the fullest extent that it is possible to live in that way after he has been sentenced for a crime, in the hope that his activity within the community will lead him to the

June 1, 1973
Penitentiaries, Parole and Temporary Absence point of rehabilitation. It flies in the face of the concept that there is no rehabilitation possible in a penitentiary. This is a point the minister seems to miss. The penitentiary is for purposes of custody; rehabilitation takes place outside and afterwards, and not within the penitentiary. The idea that if you keep a person inside for a longer period he will thereby become more amenable to rehabilitation is arrant nonsense.
The minister talks in terms of an additional expansion of the number of classification officers, visiting officers and corresponding officers. Generally-and this does not apply to every individual who falls within these categories-professional social workers who spend their time going through universities getting a degree in social work are not much help as classification officers or persons working as visiting or corresponding officers within penitentiaries because they do not know what life in a jail is all about, and they talk to inmates using a concept of language that differs from what the inmate understands. I think this step is doomed to be less than helpful, though it will no doubt build up the bureaucracy within the system.
Additional staff facilities, such as showers and lounge rooms, will not help build up the morale of the staff within the system. They are disenchanted for two reasons, basically. First, they are custodial officers who see their function being overridden by classification officers who, most of the time, do not know what they are doing anyway. Second, there is a conflict, a disenchantment, because staff custodial officers feel the people in the headquarters office do not know what they are doing either. In this regard, the first thing I think the minister should do is take some steps to replace the commissioner, Mr. Faguy. I have no complaint about Mr. Faguy's administrative competence. I am sure it is very great. But he has no idea about penological matters or prison systems. He is a professional civil servant, and his concern is with administrative structures without regard to the fact that people are within them. I would take him out of there and put somebody in who knows something about prisons and about human beings.
I have very grave doubts about the value of the correctional investigator, regardless of who fills the office, and her effectiveness in dealing with grievances by inmates. If the warden sends somebody to the hole, is the correctional officer to step into that picture and override the decision of warden's court? Certainly not. I hope not, in any event. What about the question of lost remission? What about the question of lost privileges? What about the question of discipline within a penitentiary? All we are likely to see here, following the appointment of this correctional investigator, is an advancing bureaucracy, the setting up of a further level of government structure to confuse inmates, confuse the staff, and create more general public confusion than exists at present.
The minister's statement indicates that he has not yet understood what is involved in a prison or penological system. He seeks to make the ideas contained in this statement available to all institutions. He seems to ignore the fact of life that programs applicable to one prison are not applicable in the same way to another. Surely the minister is not telling us that the program with respect to day parole should apply equally at Joyceville, which is a
{Mr. Howard.]
minimum security institution in Ontario, and at the special detention or special correctional unit just outside St. Vincent de Paul in Quebec. In our prison system what we need is not a furtherance of the so-called traditional or historic liberal approach-and I use a small "1" here, Mr. Speaker. We need one that is sensible, one that is just, one that is fair. And the two are not compatible. As long as he continues to ignore the fact that jail is for custody and that rehabilitation takes place only outside the jail and has its best opportunity for success when the citizenry are drawn into it, we shall continue to encounter difficulties, problems, abuses and, hopefully, a change of minister.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT BY SOLICITOR GENERAL OF NEW PAROLE AND TEMPORARY ABSENCE REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in accordance with the recommendations that you have often made, I will be very brief.
I would like first to congratulate the hon. minister for being kind enough to respect the bilingual character of this House and give me a French copy of his statement. I am all the more pleased to say so as last night, in committee, such was not my opinion. As a matter of fact, I blamed the hon. minister who previously had not respected the bilingual character of this country.
As far as the minister's statement is concerned, I must say that at first sight it seems acceptable to me. Ever since I became a member of the House, I have heard discussions about problems of parole prison escapes. Several members have not only made suggestions but have proposed solutions designed to improve the living conditions of prisoners in penitentiaries and to make their rehabilitation easier so that, once they are back into society, they become good citizens and help it to improve their living conditions, in order to enable our country to take full advantage of all its human resources.
Every so often, officers, prison guards are blamed for not carrying out their supervisory duties, for not doing their job, and sometimes even for deliberately taking part in some of those escapes. Personally, I am convinced that it certainly must not be easy to be a guard in a penitentiary, to live in such difficult conditions, under constant pressure.
Therefore, according to the minister's statement, today, he wants to have better living conditions for our officers, and our prison guards, allowing them to live a more normal life while doing their duty, and accepting their responsibilities. I think that this will also enable them to create a more congenial atmosphere for our inmates who no doubt have not been locked up in the penitentiary just to have a good time. They cannot expect to lead a completely normal life. If they are in there, it is because they have done something wrong, because they have violated the law and also, because order must prevail in our society.
Therefore, it is not out of nastiness or revenge that the state decrees penalties but to make sure that law is respected in the land. If the action that the minister intends to take to correct this situation appears effective, and if it is actually implemented, I am convinced that there will be considerable improvements.

Another point on which I would like to draw the attention of the minister, and I regret that he did not mention it in his statement, is the drug problem in our penitentiaries. This does not help create a responsible climate among our inmates. On the contrary, it helps to make it worse, and supervision should be more rigid in that area so that those who violate the law and who find ways of introducing drugs into our penitentiaries, be made to join those who are inside the walls, and this would help our society correct a situation which is fast becoming alarming.
When inmates have the advantage of being paroled, our society should enable them to reintegrate it easily, welcome them generously, and facilitate their rehabilitation. We must do our share. And to do our share we must act. The government is now responsible in a large part for the situation in which we are.
There is an old proverb that says: Idleness is at the root of all evil. If it is true, let us manage so that there will be fewer idle people. Conversely, one can say that work is the remedy for all evil.
Let us therefore do our utmost so that there will be more jobs in our country, so that there will be more people at work; and when there will be more people at work every day, there will be fewer inmates in the prisons.

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in moving this resolution, outlined the approach that this government is proposing to solve the problems that linguistic pluralism poses to Canada.
Canada is not, of course, the only country faced with the challenge of ensuring that two official languages do enjoy equality of status and equal rights and privileges as to their use in all government institutions. In Canada, Mr. Speaker, the passage of the Official Languages Act made this the law. It is part of this law that Canadians should be able to receive services from, and communicate with, their government in the official language of their choice. Why is this required? Quite simply to allow the 18 million Canadians who are unilingual to remain unilingual. That is the right of every Canadian. And that is why the Public Service which serves all Canadians must be able to provide its services in both English and French.
Faced with this responsibility, it is encouraging that most Canadians understand this need and the government, public servants and the staff associations which represent most employees are prepared to adopt the traditionally reasonable Canadian approach to solving this complex linguistic issue-an approach exemplified by the late respected former prime minister of Canada, Lester Pearson, who laid the foundations for bilingualism within the public service.

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext: It sure got screwed up.

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Simply stated, Mr. Speaker, if the government and the Public Service of Canada cannot meet the needs of the country by providing services in both languages and, if the public service can not be a place where both language groups can work together, both in the language of their choice, then we will have indeed failed to find a solution to the problems that linguistic pluralism poses to Canada. The price of failure for Canada is too high and is one that, I am sure all members of this House will join me in saying, is unacceptable.
Official Languages

That is my concern as President of the Treasury Board and as the minister responsible for implementing bilingualism in the Public Service.
What is involved in the first part of the resolution under study dates back to December 14, 1972 when I made a statement setting forth the government policy on bilingualism in the Public Service of Canada, the principles underlying the implementation of that policy and its effects on all Canadian citizens whether they are public servants or not.
As I said before, the principles set forth in today's resolution follow from the government policy on official languages which, even if it is well known by some, might have been forgotten or misunderstood by others.

A public service for all Canadians whether they are members of the public or public servants: that short phrase summarizes the goal of the resolution. However, without a more sustained effort to produce a greater use of the French language at all levels in the public service, without good will and a conscious, constructive effort to achieve this objective, this country will find itself with a central institution, its public service, that has little or no meaning for a large number of its citizens. To ensure that the public service has the same meaning for French speaking Canadians as it has for English speaking Canadians, Mr. Speaker, is the objective of the second part of the resolution.
Unfortunately, the government's language policies have often been misunderstood. Misunderstanding seems to be endemic to this complex and often emotionally charged subject. This resolution apparently is no exception to the rule. Various interpretations have already been read into it by some members of the House and some members of the press. Before discussing in greater detail the substance of the resolution, I would like to make clear two points.
First, it is not the government's intention to increase the use of French-or English for that matter-at all levels in the public service in all parts of Canada. Mr. Speaker, I underline the words "in all parts of Canada". In the statement that I made in December, it will be seen that the development of a functionally bilingual public service that is providing equality of opportunity for public servants at all levels to work within the public service in either English or French-will essentially be limited to the national capital region, and other such areas where both official languages are in relatively common use, both in government offices and in the surrounding communities. Given today's geographical distribution of English and French speaking Canadians, these areas would presently include such places as Montreal, certain other parts of Quebec, parts of eastern and northern Ontario, and parts of northern and eastern New Brunswick. For most of Ontario, many areas in Quebec and in most of eastern and western Canada bilingualism will only be required to meet the provisions of the Official Languages Act; but in these areas it will not be required throughout the hierarchy of the public service. I want to make this quite clear.

June 1, 1973
Official Languages

I would like to make a few remarks about another matter. It concerns the realization, in the Public Service and within the scope of the merit concept, of the full participation of members of the anglophone and francophone communities. Certain people have seen in this objective the appearance of a quota system designed to increase the number of francophone public servants to about 28 per cent, which would represent the approximate percentage of French-speaking Canadians compared with the population of Canada. That is not the case.
The government intends to ensure wider use of French in the Public Service by increasing the number of French language units, by improving the recruiting effort of the Public Service Commission, by increasing the number of professional training and administration programs offered in French and, finally, through co-operation with the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, to enhance the bilingual aspect of the national capital area. I am convinced that when all those objectives will be realized, francophones will experience more satisfaction working in the Public Service of Canada, and that their number will increase. Thus, we will have attained our objective, which is to obtain the full participation of the English-and French-speaking communities.

If then one objective is to increase the use of French within the public service, the public service must in itself become functionally bilingual. Functional bilingualism is the expression best suited to describe the aims of the nine principles, Mr. Speaker. However, to avoid these words being misunderstood, I would like to outline for the House exactly what they mean.
More precisely, functional bilingualism in the public service means that the structures of the public service should provide those in it, and those who aspire to join it, with the opportunity of choosing freely to remain unilingual while still enjoying satisfying carriers or, in cases where bilingualism is required, by offering unilinguals the opportunity of becoming bilingual, not only, Mr. Speaker, to meet their job requirements but to provide them with the means to expand their personal horizons and appreciate more fully the bilingual nature of Canada. The main points of the plan are now in front of us. Their implementation requires the good will of individuals, the talents of managers, the support of staff associations, and, the approval of this parliament.
The policy of developing a functionally bilingual public service has been supported, I am sure, by most Canadians. But at the same time, apprehensions have been aroused, individually as well as collectively. Many Canadians, and particularly public servants, were concerned about the policy because the details as to how it would be implemented had not been developed and explained clearly enough. It was not that they disagreed with the policy, but each further step appeared to them to be nearing the moment when they would have to become bilingual. Such a misunderstanding gives rise to a fear that individuals' rights would be infringed, in the name of bilingualism; of a fear, also, that measures to achieve bilingualism would jeopardize the security of employment of many conscientious and dedicated public servants. These fears, shared
(Mr. Drury.]
by many English-speaking Canadians, should now be allayed.

If it is true that English-speaking Canadians felt somewhat apprehensive, the majority of French-speaking Canadians for their part had come to mistrust the bilingualism program because progress was slow, especially in the part of the program that consisted in making the higher echelons of the Public Service capable of efficiently supervising those who wanted to work in French. Each new measure gave them the impression of becoming increasingly involved in a situation which was strange to them. They feared that the use of French would be limited to bilingual positions, even if this was contrary to the principle of equal status and rights provided for in the Official Languages Act. To them, a bilingual person is first of all a French-speaking Canadian who can work in English! To them, the concept of functional bilingualism has been created to calm this fear and mistrust by increasing the use of French as a working language to the same extent as English in the Public Service. This, Mr. Speaker,-I repeat once again-in some regions of Canada where the two language groups are significantly represented.
The government looks to the principles on bilingualism in the public service as an important milestone in the implementation of the policy on official languages; in direct continuity with the statement by the late Prime Minister, Lester B. Pearson in 1966; with the Official Languages Act of 1969, which received the support of all parties in this House and with the statement of the Prime Minister in 1970 relating to Book III of the Report of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism. Nevertheless, as indicated in the Speech from the Throne at the opening of the present session, the government feels that the House should be given the opportunity of expressing its views with the purpose of achieving a consensus on the principles.
I am pleased to inform the House that the staff associations of the public service were continuously consulted from the date of my announcement of the principles with regard to the development of the Treasury Board guidelines that give administrative application to the principles.
I would like to make special mention of the forum in which these consultations took place, the National Joint Council. The achievements of this unique organization are too numerous to enumerate here. Members of both sides of this House interested in the subject of staff relations in the public service are well acquainted with them. I would merely wish for the record to state my own satisfaction with the manner in which the National Joint Council rose to the occasion of ensuring effective consultation on this most complex and potentially divisive subject. A permanent committee of the National Joint Council will be established to provide a continuing forum for consultation on official language matters.
The guidelines on the language requirements of positions, as they now stand ready to be circulated by the Secretary of the Treasury Board, bring to the principles
June 1, 1973

only greater precision of detail with regard to the timetable of their implementation, the sectors and areas of application, the specific procedures protecting the jobs and careers of unilingual employees, the necessary mechanism of on-going consultation with the parties concerned and the setting of priorities for access to language training.
The first two principles cover the identification of the language requirements of all jobs in the public service. Principles three, four and five relate to the procedures for staffing positions in the public service with respect to language requirements. The last four principles cover the entitlement of individuals.
No one principle in those nine is more important than another, Mr. Speaker, and all are inseparable from the notion of a public service for all Canadians. In the resolution before you, the principles are derived from two fundamentals: first, Canadians should be able to receive service from, and to communicate with, the federal government in either English or French, whichever is the language of their choice. Second, Canadians who work for the Government of Canada should be able, as a general rule, to work in the language of their choice.

It is interesting to note that although most Canadians have supported these proposals there was a clearly divided reaction to implementation policies. Some Frenchspeaking Canadians considered those policies as slowing down efforts to create a functionally bilingual Public Service; although many English-speaking Canadians reacted favourably in view of the fact that the proposals supplied the clarification and the guarantees they wanted, some felt that implementation of bilingualism should be postponed for some three years. I believe that all those who felt that the policies would slow down or delay creation of a bilingual Public Service were mistaken since instead of considering the policies as a whole they considered them in isolation. Let me clarify this point.

I would like to make a clear distinction in the difference between the 1975 target percentages for bilingual employees for each occupational category, first proposed by the Public Service Commission and subsequently confirmed in the management objectives for bilingualism in the public service which I announced before the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates in March 1971, and the 1978 deadline for designation of bilingual positions. Far from being one other change, this process will mark an important turning point; accelerating previous efforts to achieve a proper form of functional bilingualism in the Public Service of Canada.
The 1975 figure refers to numbers of people in each occupational category who should be bilingual by 1975, irrespective of whether they are in positions that require bilingualism. The 1978 date refers to positions that require knowledge of both official languages and that should generally be filled by that date by bilingual persons. Using the executive category as an example, the 1975 target called for 60 per cent of those in that category to become bilingual; the 1978 deadline will require 90 per cent of the positions to be occupied by bilinguals, a somewhat different picture and hardly a slowing down of our efforts. I
Official Languages
should add, however, that the same increase in the number of those who will be required to become bilingual will not occur in other categories. The effect on the executive category is strongly influenced by the fact that most of these positions are in Ottawa. Why then the 1978 target date for the designation of bilingual positions? The answer is critical to the issue in point.
The 1975 targets aimed at achieving a pool of bilingual individuals, irrespective of the language requirement of their jobs. This posed a management problem in so far as it made it difficult to evaluate the benefit language training was bringing the public service in its day-to-day bilingual profile. After two years of closely monitoring bilingualism, the conclusion became clear. The successful achievement of the targets for 1975 would not induce or guarantee the realization of the complete list of all 11 objectives for bilingualism in the public service which I outlined to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates in March 1971. The successful development of bilingual skills in individuals does not lead to the achievement of a functionally bilingual public service. This development must be related to jobs where these skills are required and can be used.
